 Hundreds of thousands of households have had Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits stolen through electronic fraud as most states still rely on payment cards that use vulnerable magnetic-stripe technology, according to a new Food Research & Action Center (FRAC) report. The problem has become more consequential because the federal authority that reimbursed electronically stolen benefits has expired while states face mounting costs to upgrade their EBT systems. More than 36 million people received SNAP in July 2026, and most recipients remain dependent on magnetic-stripe cards as the federal government and states work toward a broader transition to chip-enabled technology. States approved nearly 769,000 claims and replaced more than $360 million in stolen SNAP benefits between January 2023 and March 2025 under the temporary federal replacement program, according to the FRAC report, which analyzed USDA data. FRAC cautioned that these figures do not capture the full extent of theft because they reflect approved replacement claims rather than every incident. Gina Plata-Nino, FRAC's director of SNAP policy and advocacy and a co-author of the report, told Newsweek that outdated payment technology has allowed criminals to target recipients through skimming, card cloning, phishing and automated attacks. "These figures capture approved replacements, not all theft, and likely understate losses," Plata-Nino said of the federal data. "Households are losing their grocery budget without having money to replace it." Why SNAP EBT Cards Remain Vulnerable to Theft The central security problem is technological. While banks have largely moved consumers onto EMV chip cards, SNAP EBT cards in most states still use magnetic stripes. Criminals can copy information encoded on a magnetic stripe, use skimming equipment to steal card data and PINs, and create counterfeit cards. Chip cards instead generate transaction data that is considerably harder to reproduce. The threat extends beyond physical skimmers. FRAC identified phishing emails, fraudulent text messages and phone calls, automated attacks on EBT systems and compromised retailer credentials among the methods used to obtain or spend benefits. The report said the predictable schedule of benefit deposits can compound the danger because criminals can drain an account shortly after the money arrives. Plata-Nino said that the exposure is greatest among recipients who still carry magnetic-stripe cards, which she said is most of the country. The consequences also fall heavily on households with children, older adults or people with disabilities. FRAC, citing USDA data, said nearly 80 percent of SNAP households include at least one person in those groups. California provides one indication of what changing the underlying technology could accomplish. The state became the first to complete a transition from magnetic stripe-only EBT cards to chip-and-tap cards in early 2025. FRAC said reported theft across California's cash and SNAP EBT programs subsequently fell 83 percent between January 2024 and late 2025, although the state also deployed other anti-fraud measures during that period. In a statement to Newsweek, USDA pushed back on criticism over the slow pace of modernization, blaming the Biden administration and states for delays. “After years of inaction by the Biden Administration, the Department publicized its proposed rulemaking to modernize the nation’s EBT system for SNAP, including the requirement of chip-enabled cards that significantly decrease instances of benefit skimming, cloning, and other theft,” a USDA spokesperson said. The department said the changes would reduce stolen benefits by at least $1.5 billion over the next decade and provide stronger protections for recipients, retailers and taxpayers. USDA also criticized states for not acting sooner, saying they had access to federal administrative money that could be used to address benefit theft. “Yet few acted,” the spokesperson said. “It is time for States to better protect food stamp recipients and the American taxpayer funding this nearly $100 billion-per-year program.” What Happens When SNAP Benefits Are Stolen? For many recipients, there is no longer a federal financial backstop. Federal statutory authority to replace electronically stolen SNAP benefits expired December 20, 2024, meaning benefits stolen beginning December 21 are not eligible for replacement using federal funds. USDA advises recipients to report stolen benefits to their state agencies, but whether money can actually be replaced now depends on state policy and funding. Plata-Nino said California and Maryland are among the states providing reimbursement on a limited basis. FRAC's state-by-state analysis shows that most states no longer replace stolen benefits, leaving substantially different outcomes depending on where a recipient lives. That is a particularly significant difference from the experience of many conventional banking customers. FRAC noted that EBT transactions were excluded from consumer protections that apply to commercial electronic transfers, leaving SNAP recipients without equivalent statutory safeguards when fraud occurs. Michael Ryan, a financial educator, told Newsweek that the loss can immediately spill into the rest of a household's finances. "For a family already stretched thin, there's NO cushion for this," Ryan said. "Say $400 in benefits disappears the day it posts. That's the month's groceries gone in minutes." The food bill, however, does not disappear with the benefits. "Usually it's the credit card. Or a utility bill gets pushed back. Or the family borrows just to eat," Ryan said. "Then the late fees and interest show up. And those can follow a household for months." The sums involved can represent much of a family's monthly grocery budget. The average SNAP household received about $341 per month in fiscal 2024, according to the FRAC report, while the average household receiving benefits had gross monthly income of $1,117 and net monthly income of $551. Which States Are Most Exposed to SNAP Theft? The problem is nationwide, but the available federal data reveals large differences among states. FRAC's analysis found particularly large numbers of claims in New York, California and Maryland during their federal reporting windows. New York reported 165,576 claims worth about $87.6 million, while California reported 115,011 claims worth about $55.6 million and Maryland reported 64,372 claims worth about $24.7 million. Those numbers should not be treated as a current ranking of where theft is worst. States reported over different periods, the federal reimbursement program ended, and USDA is no longer collecting comprehensive nationwide replacement data. FRAC said the combination makes it difficult to establish the current scale or geographic distribution of theft. Technology also varies sharply by state. FRAC's November report lists Alabama as having moved to chip-enabled cards, alongside California, while several states, including Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, Oklahoma and Virginia, have implemented, begun implementing or are piloting chip cards. Others remain at the legislative or planning stage. The patchwork means geography can determine the security technology protecting a recipient and the options available once a theft occurs. Why EBT Chip Card Modernization Is Taking So Long Moving every state to secure EBT cards is more complicated than simply mailing replacement cards. States must coordinate changes involving EBT processors, card vendors, retailers and payment terminals. National technical standards for chip-enabled EBT cards were developed before the current rollout, and retailers also need compatible point-of-sale systems for the technology to work as intended. "Federal delays and uneven state capacity have compounded that challenge," Plata-Nino said. The financial hurdle is substantial. FRAC's report, citing USDA estimates, puts state implementation costs for chip technology at roughly $2 million to $11.5 million depending largely on caseload. It estimates an individual chip-and-tap EBT card costs $2.31 to $4.99, compared with approximately 20 to 40 cents for a traditional magnetic-stripe card. Those investments are arriving as states shoulder a greater share of SNAP administration expenses. FRAC said the federal administrative reimbursement rate is declining from 50 percent to 25 percent, leaving states responsible for 75 percent, while additional benefit cost-sharing requirements are due to take effect beginning in fiscal year 2028. Plata-Nino said that those competing obligations could make security upgrades still harder to prioritize. Chip Cards Are Coming, but the Gap Remains The transition is moving forward. USDA has been working on EBT modernization and has told SNAP retailers to update their point-of-sale systems as chip-and-tap cards roll out. The agency said modernization, including introducing chip cards, is an important step toward protecting benefits. FRAC said USDA's proposed security rule would require upgraded cards using chip and near-field communication technology as well as stronger security measures and access for recipients to information about card transactions and PIN changes. The report said states would have two years after a final rule is published to implement the chip and NFC requirements. But stronger cards will not defeat every form of theft. Chip technology directly addresses vulnerabilities behind skimming and cloning, while phishing and other attacks designed to trick recipients into revealing credentials require additional protections. Plata-Nino said chip cards should therefore be accompanied by better theft reporting, stronger account controls and other measures targeting electronic fraud. The report calls on Congress to permanently restore federal replacement of electronically stolen benefits, fund nationwide EBT modernization, and strengthen data collection and consumer protections. It also argues that security should be built into the payment infrastructure instead of relying primarily on recipients to repeatedly change PINs, lock cards and monitor transactions. For Ryan, the central problem is the period between the disappearance of the federal reimbursement guarantee and widespread deployment of better technology. "Meanwhile, the replacement money is already gone," he said. "In most states right now, a family can lose a month of food money and nothing stands behind it. "Chips are coming. The question is how many months of food money disappear before they get here." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Dave Siminoff.
